title: *CS602 – GDB Solution*
text:
*CS602 – GDB Solution*

*In my opinion, Low-polygon models are more suitable* for real-time video games and interactive simulations. These applications must maintain smooth frame rates of 30 to 60 FPS on limited consumer hardware. Fewer polygons mean less vertex processing, lower memory usage, shorter rendering time, and better computational performance, which is critical for mobile, VR, and low-end GPUs. High-poly models offer superior visual accuracy, but their heavy geometry increases memory demands, slows rendering, and can exceed hardware limits, causing lag.

The trade-off is balance: use low-poly base meshes and recover visual quality through normal maps, tessellation, and Level-of-Detail (LOD), applying high detail only when objects are near the camera and low detail at a distance. This keeps performance stable while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity. High-poly modelling is better reserved for offline or pre-rendered work, where real-time constraints do not apply.

title: *Cs602 GDB Solution*
text:
*Cs602 GDB Solution*
In my opinion a balanced approach is better, but if I have to choose one, low-polygon models are more suitable for real-time games and interactive simulations.

High-polygon models give better visual quality and smooth surfaces, but they need more memory and more processing from the CPU and GPU. This increases rendering time and can lower the frame rate, so the game becomes slow or laggy. Real-time applications need around 30 to 60 frames per second, so performance is very important. Also many users have average hardware, and a heavy model may not run properly on it.

Low-polygon models use less memory and render faster, so they run smoothly on most devices. Their shape may look rough, but this can be improved with texture mapping, normal maps and shading, which add detail without adding many polygons.

The trade-off is between quality and speed. Developers can use level of detail, so high-polygon models are used for close objects and low-polygon models for far objects.
